Abstract
With the urgent demand for high-performance energy storage materials in the global energy transition, traditional experi-
mental trial and error methods are difficult to meet the rapid research and development needs owing to long cycles and high 
costs. In recent years, the deep integration of computational materials science and artificial intelligence (AI) technology 
has provided revolutionary tools for the rational design and performance optimization of energy storage materials. This 
article systematically reviews the progress of research on energy storage material computation and AI systems. At the tradi-
tional method level, quantum mechanics computation (such as VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO), molecular dynamics (such as 
LAMMPS, GROMACS), and high-throughput computing platforms (such as Materials Project) have achieved accurate pre-
dictions of material electronic structure, interface dynamics, and high-throughput screening. At the AI-driven level, genera-
tive models (GNoME, 3D-GPT), graph neural networks (MEGNet, CGCNN), and experimental computational closed–loop 
systems (such as the autonomous driving laboratory A-Lab) have significantly accelerated the discovery and reverse design 
of new materials. Further focusing on the integration trend of multi-scale modeling and AI, physical information-driven AI 
models (DPMD, PINNs) and cross-scale integration platforms (ASE, MedeA) are driving the collaborative improvement 
of material simulation accuracy and efficiency. However, data scarcity, computational bottlenecks caused by multi-physics 
coupling, and barriers to tool industrialization remain current challenges. In the future, sustainable design paradigms, open-
source ecological construction, and human-machine collaboration models will lead the research and development of energy 
storage materials into the era of “digital priority.” This article aims to provide a technical roadmap reference for interdisci-
plinary research and call for collaboration between academia and industry to overcome key bottlenecks and accelerate the 
innovation breakthrough and large-scale application of energy storage materials.

Introduction
Under the global energy transition wave, the rapid devel-
opment of renewable energy-dominated power systems, 
electric vehicles, and distributed energy networks have put 
unprecedented demands on high-performance energy stor-
age materials. Electrochemical energy storage technolo-
gies such as lithium-ion batteries, sodium sulfur batteries, 
and solid-state batteries require electrode and electrolyte 
materials with higher energy density and longer cycle 
life.1 Supercapacitors pursue fast charging and discharg-
ing and high power density; the thermal storage system 
relies on efficient phase change materials to achieve effi-
cient storage and release of thermal energy.2 However, 
traditional material development relies on experimental 
trial and error methods, which have bottlenecks such as 
long cycles (usually decades), high costs (huge single 
experiment expenses), and limited trial and error space 
(limited by chemical intuition and experience).3 For exam-
ple, optimizing the ion conductivity of solid electrolyte 
materials often requires hundreds of synthesis and char-
acterization iterations, greatly delaying the technology’s 
commercialization process. In this context, the deep inte-
gration of computational materials science and artificial 
intelligence (AI) technology provides a disruptive tool for 
the rational design of energy storage materials.4 Multi-
scale simulation methods based on quantum mechanics 
and molecular dynamics, such as VASP and LAMMPS, 
can reveal material structure performance relationships at 
the atomic level, accurately predict key properties such 
as ion migration pathways and interface stability; high 
throughput computing platforms, such as the Materials 
Project, improve material screening efficiency by several 
orders of magnitude through automated processes and 
shared databases.5 At the same time, AI technology breaks 
through the dimensional limitations of traditional simula-
tion methods through data-driven paradigms: generative 
models (such as GNoME) can explore unknown chemical 
spaces and reverse engineer materials that meet specific 
performance requirements; Graph neural networks (such 
as CGCNN) can correlate material structure with macro-
scopic properties, achieving fast property prediction; the 
experimental computational closed-loop system (such as 
A-Lab) forms an autonomous iterative loop of “design 
validation optimization” through robot experiments and 
AI feedback.
This article focuses on the technological progress of 
energy storage material calculation and AI systems, sys-
tematically sorting out the technical routes and applica-
tion scenarios of two core methods: (1) traditional com-
puting tools: covering multi-scale modeling methods 
such as quantum mechanics calculations (such as density 
functional theory, DFT), molecular dynamics (MD), and 
phase field simulations, analyzing their unique advantages 
in analyzing the electronic structure of electrode materi-
als, predicting electrolyte interface behavior, and studying 
phase transition dynamics. (2) AI-driven system: analyze 
the innovative applications of generative models, graph 
neural networks, reinforcement learning, and other algo-
rithms in material discovery, property prediction, and 
reverse design, and explore the role of experimental com-
putational closed-loop systems in reconstructing R and 
D paradigms. By comparing the applicability scenarios 
of different technologies, such as DFT being suitable 
for atomic-level accuracy but requiring high computing 
power, and AI models being longer than high-throughput 
screening but dependent on data quality, this article aims 
to provide a theoretical basis for material researchers in 
method selection and integration. Furthermore, this article 
emphasizes the potential for interdisciplinary integration: 
AI models driven by physical information, such as PINNs, 
can balance data efficiency and physical interpretability by 
embedding first principles equations.6 Cross-scale inte-
gration platforms (such as MedeA) can achieve full chain 
performance prediction from atomic to device level by 
coupling quantum mechanics, molecular dynamics, and 
phase field models.7,8
The significance of this review lies in: (1) academic level: 
integrate fragmented technology routes, reveal the theoreti-
cal framework of multi-scale modeling and AI integration, 
and provide direction for the development of new algorithms 
such as small sample learning and transfer learning; (2) at 
the industrial level: analyze industrial solutions such as Cit-
rine Informatics and MatSci ML to promote the penetration 
of computing tools from the laboratory to engineering sce-
narios; (3) at the societal level: advocate for a sustainable 
design paradigm (such as resource abundance and recy-
clability index calculation) to promote green innovation in 
energy storage materials under the goal of carbon neutrality.
Through a systematic review of technological progress 
and challenges, this article calls on academia, industry, and 
policymakers to collaborate in breaking through data barri-
ers, computing power bottlenecks, and tool usability barri-
ers, and jointly promote the development of energy storage 
materials into a new era of “digital priority.”
Application of Traditional Calculation 
Methods in Energy Storage Materials
Quantum Mechanics Calculations
Quantum mechanics calculations are based on first princi-
ples and directly reveal the intrinsic properties of materi-
als at the atomic scale by solving the Schrödinger equation,

and ion migration mechanism of energy storage materials.9

laws of electronic and material motion, thereby providing

properties, and thermodynamic and kinetic behavior of

By calculating the adsorption energy and diffusion path 
of metal ions, their stability and migration characteristics 
in materials can be predicted, providing a theoretical basis 
for the design of battery materials. First-principles calcula-
tions are also widely used in the study of complex material 
systems, such as high-pressure properties, phase diagram 
calculations, and adsorption and storage properties of porous 
carbon materials.12 For example, under high-pressure condi-
tions, first-principles calculations can predict the structural 
stability of materials and changes in their electronic proper-
ties, providing theoretical guidance for high-pressure experi-
ments.10 By calculating the electronic properties of the pore 
structure and surface active sites in porous carbon materials, 
their applications in gas storage and pollutant control can be 
optimized.13
With the development of computing technology, the 
first principles of computing have gradually shifted from 
traditional laboratory research to data-driven standardized 
process models.14 By combining databases and high-per-
formance computing platforms, researchers can efficiently 
conduct large-scale material screening and performance 
prediction. For example, material calculation software 
based on databases such as MongoDB can support the 
full process research from material design to performance 
optimization.15
The application of first-principles calculations in energy 
storage material research is not limited to battery materials 
but also includes the development of new energy systems. 
For example, in the secondary battery system, first-prin-
ciples calculations can optimize the positive and negative 
electrode materials of lithium-ion batteries, improving their 
energy density and cycling stability.10,16 In addition, first-
principles calculations can also be used to develop low-cost, 
high-performance potassium ion batteries, providing support 
for the widespread application of renewable energy.17
First-principles calculations, as a theoretical tool based on 
the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics, provide 
strong theoretical support for the research on energy storage 
materials. By accurately describing the electronic structure 
and dynamic behavior of materials, first-principles calcula-
tions can not only reveal the intrinsic properties of materials 
but also guide the design and performance optimization of 
new materials, promoting the development and application 
of energy storage technology.
VASP (Vienna Ab‑initio Simulation Package, Business 
Software)
VASP (Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package), as an efficient 
computational software based on density functional theory 
(DFT), is widely used in the field of materials science, 
especially in the electronic structure analysis of electrode 
materials and solid electrolytes, owing to its high-precision 
pseudopotential method and parallel computing optimiza-
tion.18 For example, by calculating the band structure and 
density of states (DOS) of lithium cobalt oxide ­(LiCoO2), 
its charge and discharge voltage plateau can be accurately 
predicted, providing a theoretical basis for optimizing bat-
tery performance.19 In addition, DFT simulations of lithium-
ion migration pathways in solid electrolytes such as LLZO 
­(Li7La3ZrO12) can analyze the relationship between lattice 
vacancies and ion diffusion barriers, providing key informa-
tion for improving the performance of solid-state batteries.20
The application of VASP in the research of lithium-ion 
battery materials is not limited to the above cases but also 
covers more complex material systems and reaction mecha-
nisms. For example, by combining density functional theory 
(DFT) and site-based bonding methods (BV), it is possible to 
more accurately simulate the migration path of lithium ions, 
especially in complex material systems such as ­LiMn2O4.21 
Research has shown that DFT simulation results can be 
mutually validated with BV methods in certain situations. 
Still, BV methods may have deviations in some cases owing 
to the lack of consideration for lithium-ion configuration. 
Therefore, in practical applications, it is necessary to com-
bine multiple methods for comprehensive analysis.22
For the study of solid electrolytes, VASP can efficiently 
calculate the electronic structure and diffusion energy barrier

Studies have found that the interface has significant insta-

which are of great significance for optimizing the interface 
design of solid-state electrolytes.
VASP can also optimize material properties in lithium-
ion battery materials through doping modification, surface 
modification, and other methods. For example, by doping 
transition metal elements or introducing defects, the conduc-
tivity and ion diffusion rate of materials can be significantly 
improved, thereby enhancing their overall performance.24 
Research has shown that VASP calculations have signifi-
cantly improved the electronic structure and ion diffusion 
performance of doped materials, providing theoretical sup-
port for the design of high-performance lithium-ion battery 
materials.25
VASP, as an advanced computing tool, provides strong 
theoretical support for electronic structure analysis, ion 
migration mechanism research, and interface optimiza-
tion of lithium-ion battery materials through its powerful 
pseudopotential method and parallel computing capabil-
ity. These studies not only help improve the performance 
of existing materials but also promote the development of 
new high-performance battery materials, laying the founda-
tion for achieving more efficient and safer energy storage 
technologies.
Quantum ESPRESSO (Open Source Software)
Relying on a modular design to support custom calculation 
processes, commonly used for analyzing the charge distribu-
tion and structural stability of positive electrode materials 
for sodium-ion batteries (such as ­Na3V2(PO4)3), provides 
a theoretical basis for the development of low-cost and 
resource-rich materials.26
The modular design of Quantum ESPRESSO enables 
it to support user-defined calculation processes, providing 
researchers with great flexibility. For example, by combin-
ing generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and pseu-
dopotential projection enhanced wave method (PPA), the 
software can efficiently simulate the electronic structure 
and mechanical properties of materials.27 In addition, it 
also supports various computational methods such as DFT, 
electron–phonon interaction studies, and multi-body inter-
action calculations, which give it significant advantages in 
dealing with complex material systems.28
In the research of positive electrode materials for sodium-
ion batteries, Quantum ESPRESSO can provide a theoretical 
basis for the development of low-cost and resource-abundant 
materials by accurately calculating the electronic band struc-
ture, charge distribution, and lattice stability of the materi-
als. For example, by analyzing the electronic structure and 
lattice parameters of ­Na3V2(PO4)3, its electron migration 
behavior and structural changes during charge and dis-
charge processes can be revealed, thereby optimizing its 
performance.29 In addition, the software can also simulate 
the mechanical properties of materials under different condi-
tions, such as elastic modulus, shear modulus, and thermal 
expansion coefficient, which are crucial for evaluating the 
mechanical stability of materials.
The high-performance computing capability of Quantum 
ESPRESSO also enables it to run on supercomputers and 
further improve computational efficiency through hardware 
accelerators. For example, the deployment method based on 
singularity container technology can achieve efficient cross-
platform operation, thereby simplifying the implementation 
of large-scale parallel computing.8 In addition, combined 
with a GPU acceleration strategy, Quantum ESPRESSO has 
also demonstrated good scalability and performance on het-
erogeneous computing platforms.30
Quantum ESPRESSO is not only a powerful material 
simulation tool but also provides a solid theoretical founda-
tion for research in areas such as positive electrode materials 
for sodium ion batteries through its modular design and flex-
ible computational process support. Its application prospects 
in the development of low-cost and resource-rich materials 
are broad, opening up new possibilities for the research of 
future energy materials.
DFT Calculations: Electronic Structure and Key Properties
In the study of solid-state electrolytes, the migration path of 
lithium ions in sulfides (such as ­Li10GeP2S12) is calculated 
by DFT. The diffusion energy barrier (usually < 0.3 eV) is 
quantified by transition state search (NEB method), which 
can quickly screen high ion conductivity candidate materials 
and significantly reduce the number of experimental verifi-
cations.22 This method not only improves research efficiency 
but also provides theoretical support for the design of high-
performance solid-state electrolytes.
Beyond ionic transport properties, DFT calculations are 
indispensable for evaluating electronic structures critical to 
energy storage materials.31 The accurate prediction of band 
structures, density of states (DOS), and bandgaps is funda-
mental to understanding electrochemical stability, interfacial 
charge transfer, and degradation mechanisms.32 For solid

directly correlate with their electrochemical stability win-
dow—a key metric for high-voltage battery compatibility. 
However, standard LDA/GGA functionals systematically 
underestimate bandgaps owing to self-interaction errors.33 
Hybrid functionals (e.g., HSE06) and Hubbard U corrections 
(DFT + U) significantly improve accuracy for semiconduc-
tors and transition-metal oxides, while GW methods provide 
near-experimental precision, albeit at high computational 
cost.34 ​
DFT calculation plays an important role in predicting 
the diffusion energy barrier of lithium ions. For example, 
through DFT calculations, the migration path of lithium ions 
in the crystal structure and their corresponding energy bar-
riers can be accurately described.35 This calculation method 
can reveal the migration mechanism of lithium ions between 
different lattice positions, such as gap hopping, vacancy 
mechanism, etc. In addition, DFT calculations can also be 
combined with transition state search (NEB method) to 
quantify the diffusion energy barrier of lithium ions, provid-
ing a reliable theoretical basis for experimental verification.
For electrode materials, DFT-derived electronic struc-
tures elucidate redox mechanisms and voltage profiles.36 
The projected density of states (PDOS) analysis identifies 
orbital contributions to redox activity (e.g., O 2p orbitals in 
Li-rich cathodes). Band alignment at electrode/electrolyte 
interfaces—quantified by DFT-calculated band edges and 
Fermi levels—predicts side reactions and guides protective 
coating design.37 ​
In specific applications, DFT calculations have been 
widely used in the study of lithium-ion diffusion barri-
ers.38 For example, in sulfide solid electrolytes such as 
­Li10GeP2S12, DFT calculations show that lithium ions 
mainly undergo hopping migration through tetrahedral 
gaps, and their diffusion energy barriers are usually below 
0.3 eV, indicating that these materials have high ionic con-
ductivity.39 In addition, DFT calculations can also reveal the 
migration paths of lithium ions at different lattice positions 
and their corresponding energy barrier heights, guiding the 
optimization of material structures.
It is essential to validate DFT-predicted bandgaps with 
experimental measurements (e.g., UV–Vis spectroscopy, 
x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).40 For instance, 
GGA-calculated ~1.5 eV gaps in ­LixPO3N electrolytes align 
poorly with observed 4.5 eV stability windows, whereas 
HSE06 yields gaps within 0.2–0.5 eV of experimental 
values.41 ​
DFT calculations can also be combined with other meth-
ods to improve the accuracy of predictions further. For 
example, a three-dimensional (3D) bulging descriptor is a 
descriptor based on Coulomb potential and repulsive poten-
tial in electric potential, which can more accurately cap-
ture the physical properties of lithium diffusion in complex 
compounds and their changes with system chemical modi-
fications.42 In addition, the bond valence sum (BVS) model 
has also been used to screen materials with low migration 
energy barriers quickly, and its calculated results are highly 
consistent with DFT calculations.43
It is worth noting that DFT calculations can not only 
be used for predicting the diffusion energy barrier of lith-
ium ions but also for studying the diffusion of other metal 
ions, such as sodium and potassium ions. For example, in 
graphene-based materials, the migration energy barrier of 
lithium ions is similar to that of lithium ions on graphene 
and decreases with decreasing interlayer distance.44 In addi-
tion, DFT calculations can also reveal the diffusion behavior 
of metal ions under different doping conditions, providing 
theoretical support for optimizing material properties.
Complementary to dynamical properties, DFT-based 
electronic analysis provides a holistic framework for electro-
lyte and electrode design.45 Integrating bandgap predictions 
with ion transport simulations (e.g., NEB) enables simulta-
neous optimization of conductivity and stability—critical 
for next-generation energy storage systems.46
DFT calculations have important application value in 
solid-state electrolyte research. By combining transition 
state search (NEB method) with advanced descriptor models 
such as 3D corrugation descriptor and BVS model, the diffu-
sion energy barriers of lithium ions and other metal ions can 
be efficiently predicted, providing a reliable theoretical basis 
for the design and optimization of high-performance solid 
electrolytes.47 This method not only reduces the number of 
experimental verifications but also provides important theo-
retical support for the development of solid-state batteries.
Molecular Dynamics and Mesoscopic Simulation
Molecular Dynamics (MD) Simulation
By solving Newton’s equations of motion, the behavior of 
complex systems such as electrolytes and interface dynam-
ics can be studied at the nanometer to micrometer scale. 
This method can accurately describe the dynamic processes 
of microscopic particles such as atoms, molecules, or ions 
based on first principles, and therefore has important appli-
cation value in research at the nanometer to micrometer 
scale.
The core of MD simulation lies in solving Newton’s 
equations of motion through numerical integration, in order 
to obtain the dynamic evolution process of the system.48 
This process requires consideration of the interaction forces 
between particles, usually described using potential func-
tions such as the Lennard–Jones potential, TIP4P ice model, 
etc. In addition, MD simulation also needs to be combined 
with appropriate numerical algorithms (such as the Verlet

efficiency and accuracy.49
MD simulation can provide detailed information at the 
microscopic level when studying complex systems such 
as electrolytes and interface dynamics.50 For example, in 
electrolytes, MD simulations can reveal phenomena such as 
ion diffusion behavior, solvent molecule arrangement, and 
charge distribution at interfaces.51 By analyzing these micro-
scopic dynamic processes, researchers can gain a deeper 
understanding of the electrochemical properties of electro-
lytes and their application mechanisms in energy devices 
such as batteries and capacitors.
MD simulation can also be used to study material prop-
erties at the nanoscale (Fig. 2a, b, c, d, e, and f).52–55 Fig-
ure 2 explores the material properties of gold nanoparticles 
(AuNPs) at the nanoscale through molecular dynamics (MD) 
simulations, covering key characteristics such as density, 
relative viscosity, fluorescence changes, Lindemann index, 
potential energy, and specific heat capacity. Figure 2a reveals 
the variation of density ρ of gold nanoparticles with diam-
eter D, with the horizontal axis representing diameter D (in 
angstroms, Å) and the vertical axis representing density ρ (in 
kg/m3).55 As the diameter D increases, the density ρ gradu-
ally approaches the density of bulk gold, indicating that the 
density of large-sized nanoparticles tends to stabilize. Fig-
ure 2b focuses on the relationship between relative viscosity 
η/η0 and diameter D, with the horizontal axis representing 
diameter D and the vertical axis representing relative vis-
cosity η/η0.55  The relative viscosity η/η0 increases with the 
increase of diameter D, indicating that the viscosity of nano-
particles increases with size. Figure 2c and d, respectively, 
show the fluorescence changes at the core interface and tail 
interface.53 The horizontal axis of Fig. 2c lists different 
binding situations (negative control, receptor, core binding, 
etc.), and the vertical axis represents the fluorescence change 
amplitude.53 The results showed that receptor structures that 
bind only at the core interface or only at the R-p tail inter-
face can induce conformational changes at both interfaces, 
indicating the existence of interaction between the core and 
tail interfaces.
Figure 2d further supports this discovery from the per-
spective of the tail interface, showing a similar trend of 
fluorescence changes.53 As the temperature increases, the 
Lindemann index of all regions increases, indicating a 
decrease in structural stability. The Lindemann index of 
the core region rises slowly, indicating that it still maintains 
high structural stability at high temperatures. In contrast, 
the indices of the subsurface and free surface regions rise 
rapidly, indicating that these regions are more prone to struc-
tural transformation at high temperatures (Fig. 2e).54  The 
potential energy rapidly decreases and then stabilizes with 
increasing temperature, reflecting significant changes dur-
ing the melting process. The peak of specific heat capacity 
in a specific temperature range indicates the occurrence of 
a phase transition or structural transformation. At different 
heating rates, the trends of potential energy and specific 
heat capacity are similar. Still, there are differences in peak 
position and amplitude, indicating that heating rate has an 
impact on thermodynamic properties (Fig. 2f).54 Overall, 
Fig. 2 presents the physical and chemical properties of gold 
nanoparticles at different scales and conditions, providing a 
solid theoretical and experimental foundation for a deeper 
understanding and practical application of nanomaterials.
For example, in the study of nanostructure failure and 
full atomic molecular dynamics simulation, the stability 
and failure mechanism of nanomaterials under different 
conditions can be revealed by simulating the reaction 
potential between carbon atoms. In addition, MD simula-
tion is widely used in nano-machining technology, such 
as in the study of the formation mechanism of the cop-
per nanomechanical machining surface layer. By simulat-
ing the atomic motion during the machining process, the 
machining process can be optimized and the machining 
accuracy can be improved.56
MD simulation can also be combined with other compu-
tational methods, such as the Monte Carlo method (MC), to 
compensate for its limitations in certain fields. For example, 
in the study of VOC adsorption behavior on activated car-
bon, MD simulation can provide a microscopic mechanism 
of macroscopic adsorption properties. At the same time, the 
MC method can further optimize the adsorption model.57
Although MD simulation has significant advantages in 
research at the nanometer to micrometer scale, its computa-
tional cost is high, and the time scale is limited.58 To address 
these issues, researchers have proposed various improve-
ment methods. For example, the smooth molecular dynamics 
(SMD) method can expand the time scale while maintaining 
high accuracy by introducing background grids and mapping 
ideas. In addition, the MD method based on energy conver-
sion rate correction (ECBC) breaks through the application 
limitations of traditional MD methods in nonconservative 
systems by introducing a new computational framework.59
MD simulation, as a powerful computational tool, has 
made significant progress in multiple fields such as electro-
lytes, interface dynamics, and nanomaterials. In the future, 
with the improvement of computing power and optimization 
of algorithms, MD simulation will play a greater role in a 
wider range of scientific and engineering problems.

High‑Throughput Computing and Database 
Platform
High-throughput computing generates material data in 
batches through automated processes, combined with data-
base sharing mechanisms, significantly accelerating mate-
rial screening and design.81 This process not only relies on 
advanced computing technology but also on the support 
of data management and sharing platforms. For example, 
material screening methods based on high-throughput com-
puting have been widely applied in multiple fields, such as 
lithium-ion battery materials, gas separation materials, and 
the study of interfacial friction characteristics of two-dimen-
sional materials.82 These studies can quickly generate a large 
amount of physical and chemical property data of materials 
through automated calculations and data mining, providing 
a scientific basis for material design.
In terms of material data generation, high-throughput 
computing platforms typically combine first-principles cal-
culations, machine learning algorithms, and data mining 
techniques to achieve efficient prediction of material proper-
ties.83 For example, through a web-based computing process, 
material structure data can be input into first principles com-
puting software (such as VASP) and corresponding mate-
rial performance data can be generated. In addition, some 
studies have developed specialized high-throughput comput-
ing platforms, such as the MatCloud platform, to automate 
the search for optimal adsorption sites on crystal surfaces, 
thereby improving the efficiency of material screening.
However, the true value of high-throughput computing 
lies in its combination with data-sharing mechanisms. By 
establishing a shared database, researchers can centrally 
store and share the generated material data, thereby avoiding 
duplicate calculations and improving research efficiency. 
For example, a lithium-ion battery material database based 
on material genetic engineering ideas generates and shares 
computational results through a web server, providing 
researchers with efficient data access and analysis tools.84 In 
addition, the shared database design based on cloud servers 
further enhances the flexibility and real-time performance 
of data management.
In order to better support data sharing, some studies have 
also proposed synchronous replication technology on the 
basis of heterogeneous databases to address compatibility 
issues between different databases. For example, through 
distributed database technology, data synchronization and 
consistency can be achieved between multiple database sys-
tems, ensuring the accuracy and reliability of data sharing.73 
In addition, the open scientific database mechanism based on 
correlated data has also been proven to support open access 
and the effective sharing of scientific data.

AI technology has disrupted the traditional paradigm of 
material discovery by mining massive amounts of mate-

low efficiency, high costs, and long cycles. For example,

although the relationship between material performance and

retical studies, the processing of high-dimensional data and 
modeling of complex structure-activity relationships remain 
a huge challenge.99,130 In addition, traditional methods often 
struggle to achieve efficient data analysis and prediction 
when faced with large-scale data, which limits the rapid 
development of new materials.
To address these issues, the application of AI technology, 
especially machine learning (ML), has gradually become 
a research hotspot in the field of materials science.131 By 
building data-driven models, AI can quickly capture the 
complex relationships between material composition, struc-
ture, process, and performance, and significantly improve 
the efficiency of material screening and design. For exam-

ing efficiency.132 In addition, AI can also combine imaging

Active Learning Framework and Efficient Screening
The active learning strategy based on Bayesian optimization 
significantly reduces the number of experimental validations 
by dynamically balancing the “exploration utilization” trade-
off.159 For example, in solid-state electrolyte screening, with 
ion conductivity and electrochemical window as optimi-
zation objectives, only 50 iterations are needed to locate 
the optimal solution from 10 candidate materials (such as 
­Li9.54Si1.74P1.44S16Cl3), with a 90% increase in efficiency 
compared with traditional grid search.
Bayesian optimization is a method of optimization under 
uncertain conditions, whose core idea is to predict the value 
of the objective function by constructing a probability model 
and selecting the optimal experimental conditions by com-
bining sampling strategies.160 This method is particularly 
suitable for high-dimensional, nonlinear, and computation-
ally expensive optimization problems. Under the framework 
of active learning, Bayesian optimization is further applied 
to dynamically adjust sampling strategies to achieve efficient 
exploration and utilization of the objective function.161,162
Specifically, active learning frameworks typically involve 
two key steps: selecting the most valuable samples for 
experimentation and updating the model on the basis of the 
experimental results.163 In the screening of solid electrolyte 
materials, this process is manifested as: first, using Bayesian 
models to predict the performance of candidate materials, 
and then selecting materials that are most likely to approach 
the optimal solution through adaptive sampling strategies for 
experimental verification.164 After the experimental results 
are fed back, the model will be continuously updated to 
approximate the global optimal solution more efficiently.
Compared with traditional grid search methods, the 
advantage of combining Bayesian optimization with active 
learning is that it can significantly reduce the number of 
experiments.165 For example, in solid-state electrolyte 
screening, traditional methods may require traversing all 
candidate materials. At the same time, Bayesian optimiza-
tion dynamically adjusts the sampling strategy and only 
requires 50 iterations to find the optimal solution.86,166,167 
In addition, this method can effectively handle high-dimen-
sional search spaces and sparse data problems, which is par-
ticularly important in the screening of solid-state electrolyte 
materials, as material properties are often affected by mul-
tiple parameters.
However, Bayesian optimization also faces some chal-
lenges. For example, the accuracy of the model depends on 
the quality of the initial data. If the initial data is insufficient 
or has a large deviation, it may lead to unsatisfactory opti-
mization results.160,168 In addition, high-dimensional search 
spaces and complex prior assumptions may also increase the 
difficulty of model training.169 Therefore, in practical appli-
cations, researchers often combine other techniques such 
as feature selection, variable compression, etc., to optimize 
model performance.170
The active learning strategy based on Bayesian optimiza-
tion provides an efficient and flexible solution for the screen-
ing of solid electrolyte materials. By dynamically balancing 
the “exploration utilization” trade-off, this method not only 
significantly reduces the number of experiments but also 
improves screening efficiency and accuracy. Future research

AI Feedback Optimization Experiment Parameters
In the synthesis of solid-state electrolytes, AI systems rec-
ommend optimal process parameters (such as 12-h wet ball 
milling + 850°C sintering) by analyzing historical data (such 
as the correlation between ball milling time and ion con-
ductivity), resulting in an increase in the synthesis purity 
of ­Li10GeP2S12 from 82% to 95% and an increase in ion 
conductivity from 12 mS/cm to 25 mS/cm.47
From existing research, the influence of ball milling time 
on material properties exhibits significant regularity.207 For 
example, in the preparation of ­Fe3O4 hollow particles, as 
the ball milling time increases, the particles are gradually 
ground, leading to the formation of a conductive network 
and thus improving the conductivity of the material.208 Sim-
ilarly, when preparing ­Sr0.7Sm0.3Fe0.4Co0.6O2.65 perovskite 
materials, adjusting the ball milling time (0 h to 10 h) can 
significantly improve the microstructure and surface area of 
the material, thereby optimizing its optoelectronic proper-
ties. These studies indicate that ball milling time is one of 
the important factors affecting material properties.
However, the longer the ball milling time, the better. For 
example, when preparing AgI-Ag2WO4 composite materials, 
it was found that after ball milling for more than 10 h, the 
ion conductivity decreased.209 This indicates that excessively 
prolonged ball milling time may lead to damage or uneven 
distribution of the internal structure of the material, thereby 
inhibiting performance improvement. Therefore, when rec-
ommending process parameters, AI systems need to com-
prehensively consider material properties and experimental 
objectives to avoid ineffective or even harmful parameter 
combinations.
The sintering temperature is also a key factor affecting the 
performance of solid electrolytes. For example, in the prepa-
ration of ­Ce0.8Gd0.2O1.9 (CGO) solid electrolyte, a two-step 
sintering process (TSS) was used to achieve higher density 
and smaller grain size at lower temperatures, significantly 
improving conductivity.210 This indicates that the choice of 
the sintering process has a significant impact on the final 
performance.

Dynamics, and Phase Field Model
1.	 ASE (Atomic Simulation Environment)
As an open-source toolchain, ASE seamlessly connects 
first-principles calculations (such as VASP and Quantum 
ESPRESSO) with molecular dynamics (such as LAMMPS), 
supporting cross-scale data transfer.223 For example, in the 
study of lithium metal negative electrodes, the adsorption 
energy of lithium atoms on copper substrates is first calcu-
lated by DFT. Then this parameter is used as input to drive 
molecular dynamics simulations of lithium dendrite growth. 
Finally, a phase field model is used to predict the critical 
current density at which dendrites penetrate the separator.224
In the research of lithium metal negative electrode materi-
als, ASE can achieve cross-scale computational simulation 
through the following steps: (1) first-principles calculations 
(DFT): by combining ASE with first-principles calculation 
tools such as VASP or Quantum ESPRESSO, the adsorption 
energy of lithium atoms on copper substrates can be accu-
rately calculated.225 This step utilizes advanced algorithms 
of density functional theory (DFT), such as the plane wave 
pseudopotential method, which can efficiently describe the 
electronic structure and interactions at the atomic scale. In 
addition, ASE also supports exporting calculation results 
to a standard format for seamless integration with other 
modules.226 (2) Molecular dynamics simulation: after 
obtaining the adsorption energy parameters of lithium atoms 
on copper substrates, ASE can further input these parameters 
into molecular dynamics simulations,227 such as LAMMPS, 
to drive the growth process simulation of lithium dendrites. 
Molecular dynamics simulation can simulate large-scale 
dynamic behaviors, such as the diffusion of lithium ions 
in electrolytes, and the formation and evolution of lithium 
dendrites, thereby revealing the microscopic mechanisms 
of lithium dendrite growth.228 (3) Phase-field model predic-
tion: finally, ASE can integrate phase-field models to predict 
the critical current density of lithium dendrite penetration 
through membranes.229 This process requires a combination 
of experimental data and theoretical calculations to simulate 
the penetration behavior of lithium dendrites under different 
conditions by optimizing phase field parameters. The modu-
lar design of ASE enables users to adjust model parameters 
and conduct large-scale sensitivity analysis easily.
The flexibility and openness of ASE give it unique

DPMD (Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics)
Constructing potential energy surfaces based on deep neural 
networks and achieving a balance between accuracy and effi-
ciency through DFT data training.247 DPMD simulates the 
diffusion coefficient of lithium ions in polymer electrolytes 
(such as PEO LiTFSI) with a deviation of less than 15% 
from experimental values, and the calculation speed is 1000 
times faster than traditional DFT.
Beyond ionic dynamics, DPMD enables efficient struc-
tural optimization critical for electronic property evalua-
tion.248 By sampling thousands of configurations at finite 
temperatures, DPMD generates statistically robust datasets 
for calculating bandgaps.249 For example, DPMD-MD simu-
lations of ­Li3PS4 reveal a 0.3 eV bandgap reduction at 300 K 
due to thermal disorder—unattainable with static DFT. How-
ever, bandgaps inherit errors from training data; combining 
DPMD with hybrid-DFT (e.g., HSE06) achieves < 0.15 eV 
MAE versus experiments for sulfide electrolytes.250
Another key feature of the DPMD method is its ab initio 
nature. Owing to its potential energy surface being trained 
on DFT data, DPMD can preserve all-natural symmetries 
and avoid the assumptions artificially introduced in tradi-
tional empirical potential functions.248 This ab initio prop-
erty enables DPMD to have higher reliability and universal-
ity when dealing with complex material systems.
Emerging hybrid methods integrate DPMD with elec-
tronic structure calculators (e.g., DFTB +, Quantum 
ESPRESSO).251 This allows real-time bandgap tracking dur-
ing ion diffusion—revealing how ­Li+ hopping in graphite 
anodes transiently narrows interlayer bandgaps by 0.5 eV, 
accelerating electron transfer.252 ​
The application scope of DPMD is very wide, cover-
ing various research fields from solid-state materials to 
molecular systems.253 For example, in the dynamic study of 
germanium atoms on graphene/copper substrates, DPMD 
successfully simulated the effect of single-layer graphene 
on the adsorption energy of germanium atoms and revealed 
the significant enhancement of graphene’s adsorption energy 
on germanium atoms under stress regulation. In addition, 
DPMD has been used to study the dynamic behavior of 
energy-related materials, such as titanium dioxide oxygen 
vacancy diffusion.
The DPMD method provides an efficient, accurate, 
and universal solution for molecular dynamics simulation 
through the efficient fitting ability and ab initio properties of 
deep neural networks.254 It not only significantly improves 
computational efficiency but also provides new possibilities 
for the study of complex material systems, promoting pro-
gress in multiple fields such as materials science, chemistry, 
and physics.

PINNs (Physics‑Informed Neural Networks)
Partial differential equations (such as the Cahn–Hilliard 
equation of the phase field model) are used as loss func-
tion constraints to predict the phase transition behavior of 
battery electrode materials.5 For example, PINNs can accu-
rately predict NMC811 ­(LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2). The lithium 
concentration gradient distribution during the fast charging 
process has a mean square error (MSE) as low as ­10–4.
Crucially, lithium concentration gradients directly corre-
late with electronic properties via the ​drift-diffusion-Poisson 
coupling​. PINNs embedding this physics can predict band 
edge shifts during phase transitions: In NMC811, a 20% ­Li+ 
gradient causes a 0.35 eV conduction band lowering, trig-
gering oxygen loss at high voltages.255 ​
PINNs can also be further extended by introducing frac-
tional order physical information (fPINNs) to handle spati-
otemporal fractional order partial differential equations (such 
as fractional order Cahn–Hilliard equations). This extension 
method simulates more complex physical phenomena, such 
as nonuniform diffusion processes or nonlinear phase sepa-
ration processes, by introducing fractional derivatives and 
integrals.256 Research has shown that fPINNs exhibit higher 
accuracy and robustness when dealing with such problems, 
especially when dealing with systems with complex geom-
etry and boundary conditions.
PINNs can further improve computational efficiency and 
accuracy by combining other numerical methods, such as the 
finite element method (FEM) and spectral method.257 For 
example, when PINNs are combined with FEM, the struc-
tural advantages of finite element mesh can be utilized, and 
physical parameters can be automatically optimized through 
neural networks, thereby reducing computational costs and 
improving prediction accuracy. This method has been proven 
to have significant effects in dealing with heat conduction 
problems, fluid dynamics, and multiphase flow.
The application of PINNs in battery materials science has 
demonstrated its strong potential, especially in dealing with 
complex physical problems such as phase transition behavior 
and lithium-ion concentration distribution. By embedding 
physical laws into neural networks, PINNs can efficiently 
predict and optimize physical processes on the basis a small 
amount of data, providing a new tool for the design and 
optimization of battery materials.258

2.	 Virtual Experiment Platform
The BatteryDEV platform developed by NIST in the USA 
allows users to upload material composition and synthesis 
conditions, automatically generate electrochemical perfor-
mance heat maps (such as first effect energy density rela-
tionship), and reduce experimental trial and error by up to 
70%. The core advantage of virtual experiment platforms 
lies in their ability to simulate real experimental environ-
ments, reducing time and resource consumption in physical 
experiments.341 For example, the BatteryDEV platform digi-
tizes complex electrochemical reaction processes through 
computer simulation technology. Users only need to input 
the composition and preparation conditions of the materi-
als to obtain performance prediction results quickly. This 
technology not only reduces experimental costs but also 
improves the accuracy and reliability of research. In addi-
tion, the application scope of virtual experiment platforms 
is extensive, not limited to the field of batteries, but can also 
be extended to other disciplines such as materials science, 
biology, and engineering.302
From a technical perspective, virtual experiment plat-
forms are typically based on advanced computational models 
and algorithms, such as X3D-based virtual experiment plat-
forms that utilize 3D modeling technology to enable users 
to observe the experimental process and results intuitively. 
At the same time, the virtual laboratory also combines the 
remote control and sharing network architecture to real-
ize real-time data transmission and multi-user cooperation 
through the interconnection between the low-level control 
network and the internet. These technological features make 
virtual experiment platforms not only suitable for teaching 
and research in universities and research institutions but 
also meet the industry’s demand for efficient research and 
development.
The virtual experiment platform also has good openness 
and compatibility.342 For example, in the research on the 
open sharing mechanism of virtual simulation experiment 
teaching resources in universities, a management system 
with a three-tier platform organizational structure of top-
level, policy, and application has been proposed to ensure 
the effective utilization of virtual experiment resources. This 
open-sharing concept is also applicable to virtual experi-
mental platforms such as BatteryDEV, which can help pro-
mote global scientific research cooperation and technologi-
cal progress.
The development of virtual experiment platforms also 
faces some challenges. For example, how to further improve 
simulation accuracy, optimize user experience, and enhance 
system security still needs continuous improvement. How-
ever, with the continuous advancement of technologies such 
as artificial intelligence, big data, and cloud computing, the 
functions of virtual experiment platforms will become more 
complete, and their application fields will also be further 
expanded.
As a typical representative of virtual experiment technol-
ogy, the BatteryDEV platform not only plays an important 
role in battery material research but also provides new ideas 
and methods for scientific research in other fields. In the 
future, with the continuous development of technology, vir-
tual experiment platforms are expected to become important 
tools for scientific research and teaching, providing stronger 
support for human exploration of the unknown world.

The deep collaboration between AI and human experts is

1.	 AI-Assisted Experimental Decision-Making
Embedding expert rules (such as “Sulfide electro-
lytes should avoid oxygen impurities”) in the Bayesian 
optimization framework has increased the success rate 
of solid electrolyte screening from 55% to 85%. Bayes-
ian optimization is a global optimization method based 
on probabilistic models, which guides the search process 
by constructing the probability distribution of the objec-
tive function.170 This method has significant advantages 
in dealing with high-dimensional, nonconvex, and dis-
continuous problems, especially in the fields of materials 
science and engineering, which can effectively improve 
screening efficiency and success rate. However, traditional 
Bayesian optimization algorithms may not fully consider 
the experience and rules of domain experts, which may 
lead to blindness in the screening process.
By embedding expert rules into the Bayesian optimization 
framework, this problem can be significantly improved. For 
example, in the screening of solid electrolytes, sulfide elec-
trolytes need to avoid oxygen impurities, as oxygen impuri-
ties can seriously affect their performance and stability.343 
This expert rule can be expressed in the form of a Bayes-
ian network and combined with optimization algorithms. 
A Bayesian network is a probabilistic graphical model that 
can effectively represent the dependencies and uncertainties 
between variables. By transforming expert rules into a part 
of Bayesian networks, the search direction can be dynami-
cally adjusted during the optimization process to avoid solu-
tions that do not comply with expert rules.
Furthermore, by combining evolutionary computation 
methods such as genetic algorithms, the optimization effect 
can be further improved. Genetic algorithms can search 
for global optimal solutions in complex spaces by simulat-
ing natural selection and genetic mechanisms.344 Based on 
Bayesian optimization, introducing a genetic algorithm can 
utilize its powerful global search ability to compensate for 
the possible local optimal problems that may exist in rely-
ing solely on Bayesian optimization. For example, genetic 
algorithms can transform incomplete data into complete 
data through encoding and decoding network structures, 
and guide the search process through fitness functions.345 
This method can not only improve the success rate of screen-
ing but also accelerate convergence to the global optimal 
solution.
The experimental results show that by embedding expert 
rules and combining them with genetic algorithms, the suc-
cess rate of solid electrolyte screening has increased from 
55% to 85%.140 This improvement not only validates the 
effectiveness of combining Bayesian optimization with 
expert rules but also provides a reference for experimental 
decision-making in other fields. For example, in fields such 
as drone threat assessment and quantum key distribution sys-
tems, similar optimization methods can also significantly 
improve decision efficiency and accuracy.
By embedding expert rules in the Bayesian optimization 
framework and combining them with evolutionary compu-

of solid electrolyte screening can be significantly improved. 
This method not only improves experimental efficiency but 
also provides new ideas and tools for optimizing other com-
plex systems.

Conclusions
The global energy transition poses unprecedented challenges 
to the performance and large-scale application of energy 
storage materials, and the deep integration of computing 
tools and artificial intelligence (AI) systems is reshaping the 
underlying logic of material research and development. This 
article systematically demonstrates how the technological 
system from quantum mechanics computing to AI-driven 
design accelerates material discovery: traditional simulation 
methods, such as VASP and LAMMPS solve the accuracy 
problem of atomic scale mechanism analysis; AI-generated 
models (such as GNoME and diffusion models) have broken 
through the chemical space exploration boundaries of tra-
ditional trial and error methods; The experimental compu-
tational closed-loop system (such as A-Lab) bridges virtual 
design and real synthesis through robot experiments and 
dynamic feedback. These technological collaborations have 
compressed the material research and development cycle 
from a 10-year level to a monthly level, reduced costs by 
up to 80%, and promoted the emergence of breakthrough 
materials such as lithium metal negative electrodes and high 
entropy oxide electrodes.
However, the bottleneck of technology implementation 
is still significant: small sample data restricts the generali-
zation ability of AI models, high computational costs for 
cross-physical field coupling, and insufficient tool usability 
hinders industrial transformation. In this regard, this article 
proposes three core paths: (1) interdisciplinary deep inte-
gration: breaking down the disciplinary barriers between 
computational science, AI, and experimental science, 
developing physics information-driven small sample learn-
ing algorithms (such as PINNs), quantum-classical hybrid 
computing frameworks, and constructing material digital 
twin platforms to achieve full lifecycle simulation; (2) open 
source ecosystem coconstruction: promote standardized 
protocols such as OpenKIM and OMDB to be compatible 
with unstructured data, establish a shared database for enter-
prise university collaboration, and promote interoperability 
upgrades between commercial software (MedeA) and open 
source tools (ASE); (3) innovation in human-machine col-
laboration paradigm: integrating expert knowledge into AI 
decision-making (such as knowledge graph constrained gen-
erative models), and lowering the application threshold for 
frontline R and D personnel through low code/cloud-native 
tools (Citrine, MatSci ML).
The future research and development of energy storage 
materials will inevitably move towards the era of “digital 
first”: with computing and AI as pioneers, data as fuel, and 
sustainability as the navigation standard. Only by forming 
a joint force between academia, industry, and policymak-
ers, breaking through the shackles of tool isolation, frag-
mented computing power, and data fragmentation, can we 
achieve the ultimate leap from “experience trial and error” to 
“rational design” and lay the material foundation for energy 
transformation under the goal of carbon neutrality.

Abstract: With the urgent demand for high-performance energy storage materials in the global energy transition, traditional experi- mental trial and error methods are difficult to meet the rapid research and development needs owing to long cycles and high costs. In recent years, the deep integration of computational materials science and artificial intelligence (AI) technology has provided revolutionary tools for the rational design and performance optimization of energy storage materials. This article systematically reviews the progress of research on energy storage material computation and AI systems. At the tradi- tional method level, quantum mechanics computation (such as VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO), molecular dynamics (such as LAMMPS, GROMACS), and high-throughput computing platforms (such as Materials Project) have achieved accurate pre- dictions of material electronic structure, interface dynamics, and high-throughput screening. At the AI-driven level, genera- tive models (GNoME, 3D-GPT), graph neural networks (MEGNet, CGCNN), and experimental computational closed–loop systems (such as the autonomous driving laboratory A-Lab) have significantly accelerated the discovery and reverse design of new materials. Further focusing on the integration trend of multi-scale modeling and AI, physical information-driven AI models (DPMD, PINNs) and cross-scale integration platforms (ASE, MedeA) are driving the collaborative improvement of material simulation accuracy and efficiency. However, data scarcity, computational bottlenecks caused by multi-physics coupling, and barriers to tool industrialization remain current challenges. In the future, sustainable design paradigms, open- source ecological construction, and human-machine collaboration models will lead the research and development of energy storage materials into the era of “digital priority.” This article aims to provide a technical roadmap reference for interdisci- plinary research and call for collaboration between academia and industry to overcome key bottlenecks and accelerate the innovation breakthrough and large-scale application of energy storage materials.
